desc:
A one-way road network has n towns labelled 0 to n - 1. Each roads[i] = [from, to, toll] is a one-way road. A toll may be negative (a bonus paid to the driver).

A travel plan must start at town src, end at town dst and use exactly k roads. Towns and roads may be used again and again, so cycles are allowed. Return the smallest possible sum of tolls over all such plans, or 1000000000 if no plan with exactly k roads exists. With k = 0 the only plan is to stay put, which works only when src == dst and costs 0.

Because the number of roads is fixed, a cycle with negative total toll cannot be repeated forever, so the answer is always well defined.

Example: roads = [[0,1,4],[1,2,-2],[2,0,3],[0,2,5]], src = 0, dst = 2. With k = 1 the answer is 5, with k = 2 it is 2 (0 → 1 → 2), and with k = 3 it is 13 (0 → 2 → 0 → 2).
constraints: roads[i] = [from, to, toll] with 0 ≤ from, to < n, from ≠ to and -100 ≤ toll ≤ 100
Each ordered pair (from, to) appears at most once
hints: A plain shortest path would ignore the 'exactly k roads' rule, and with negative tolls you cannot just forbid revisiting towns.
Let f[j][v] be the cheapest toll total of a plan that starts at src, uses exactly j roads and ends at v. How is f[j] computed from f[j-1]?

Start with f[0][src] = 0. For each j from 1 to k, build a fresh array: for every road (u, v, t) with f[j-1][u] finite, update f[j][v] = min(f[j][v], f[j-1][u] + t). Return f[k][dst] or the 'impossible' value.
editorial: This is Bellman-Ford without the early exit and without the 'at most' relaxation: the rounds themselves are the answer. Layer j of the table stores the best cost for walks of exactly j roads. Every layer is built only from the previous one, so a road is counted once per round, and the final layer k holds the cheapest cost of walks with exactly k roads ending in each town.

Negative cycles are harmless here because a walk cannot loop more than k times; the minimum over a finite set of walks exists. That is the difference from the unrestricted shortest path problem, where a negative cycle would make the answer unbounded. Only the previous layer is needed, so space is O(n) and time is O(k · E). If k were huge (10<sup>9</sup>), the same recurrence would be done by repeated squaring of the distance matrix in the (min, +) semiring.
